content: The SHLD1 gene, also known as shieldin complex subunit 1 or C20orf196, is located on chromosome 20. It encodes an mRNA that is 1,763 base pairs in length and a protein consisting of 205 amino acids. Function C20orf196 plays a critical role in the DNA repair network. Gupta et al. identified it as a component of a vertebrate-specific protein complex called shieldin. This complex is recruited to double-stranded DNA breaks (DSBs) to facilitate repair through nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ), immunoglobulin class-switch recombination (CSR), and the fusion of unprotected telomeres. Studies suggest that SHLD1 exhibits a sub-stoichiometric interaction or weaker binding affinity within the shieldin complex. Gene Structure The SHLD1 gene spans base pairs 5,750,286 to 5,864,407 on the direct strand of chromosome 20 and contains 11 exons. Aliases The gene is also referred to as RINN3 and SHLD1. Expression mRNA C20orf196 undergoes alternative splicing, producing nine distinct mRNA variants, including seven alternatively spliced forms and two unspliced forms. These variants arise from three probable alternative promoters, three non-overlapping alternative last exons, and two alternative polyadenylation sites. The mRNA variants differ in their 5' and 3' truncations, the presence or absence of two cassette exons, and overlapping exons with different boundaries. Isoforms The gene encodes six splice isoforms. Promoter The promoter region spans 1,270 base pairs, located between bases 5,749,286 and 5,750,555. The transcription start site is within bases 5,750,382 to 5,750,409, covering 28 base pairs. Tissue Expression RNA-Seq analysis has demonstrated ubiquitous expression of C20orf196 across 26 human tissues, including the adrenal gland, appendix, bone marrow, brain, colon, duodenum, endometrium, esophagus, fat, gall bladder, heart, kidney, liver, lung, lymph node, ovary, pancreas, placenta, prostate, salivary gland, skin, small intestine, spleen, stomach, testis, thyroid, and urinary bladder. The highest mRNA levels were observed in the lymph node, tonsil, thyroid, adrenal gland, prostate, pharynx, parathyroid, connective tissue, and bone marrow. Additionally, C20orf196 is expressed in soft tissue/muscle tumors, lymphoma tumors, and pancreatic tumors. Its expression is biased toward the fetal developmental stage. EBI expression data indicate high levels in the diencephalon and cerebral cortex during brain development. Protein General Features The most common transcript encodes a protein of 205 amino acids with a molecular mass of approximately 23 kDa. The protein is predicted to have a half-life of around 30 hours. Cellular Localization C20orf196 is predicted to localize in the nucleus. Domains The protein contains a single domain, DUF4521, which originated in amniotes and spans amino acids 3 to 201. This domain is conserved among orthologs in mammals, amphibians, and fish. However, the proteins in this family remain functionally uncharacterized. Post-Translational Modifications C20orf196 is predicted to undergo several post-translational modifications, including: Multiple phosphorylation sites targeted by unspecified serine kinases. One SUMOylation site at amino acid 203. One N-glycosylation site at amino acid 69. Two ubiquitination sites at amino acids 84 and 139. Secondary Structure Modeling programs predict a secondary structure comprising alpha helices, beta sheets, and coil regions. Protein Interactions C20orf196 interacts with several proteins, including PRMT1, QARS, MAD2L2, and CUL3, as identified through yeast two-hybrid screenings. Within the shieldin complex, it functionally interacts with REV7, SHLD2, and SHLD3 as part of the DNA repair network. Homology and Evolution Orthologs Orthologs of C20orf196 are found in mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians, with distant orthologs present in bony and cartilaginous fish. No orthologs are found in invertebrates. Orthologs have been identified in 163 organisms. Paralogs There are no paralogs of C20orf196 in humans. Evolutionary Rate C20orf196 exhibits a high rate of protein sequence divergence, evolving faster than fibrinogen, making it a rapidly evolving protein. Phenotype Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the C20orf196 gene that are associated with parental longevity, information processing speed, and breast carcinoma occurrence.
